section_summary: This section covers U.S. State Department records from January to March 1944 relating to internal conditions in wartime Japan, diplomatic and press observations, and postwar civil affairs planning. Reports from journalists and recently returned Chinese students document deteriorating living conditions on the Japanese home front, including acute food and clothing shortages, intensive student and female labor mobilization, pervasive air raid dread, and declining faith in the military authorities following losses at Attu and Kiska. The materials also feature diplomatic reporting on Japanese cabinet and military command reshuffles and the complete interagency minutes and text of the political directive governing the U.S. military occupation of the Japanese Mandated Islands in the Central Pacific.

subfiles.about: A newspaper report based on an interview with an escaped Chinese resident describing declining civilian morale, food shortages, and acute fear of air raids in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Stein reports a young Chinese escapee describing collapsed public confidence after Allied Europe/Aleutian victories, severe shortages, compulsory student drilling, and predicts bombing would turn anger against Japan's government.
subfiles.title: Japan from the Inside: Hope of Victory Lost: People Living in Fear of Air Raids

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting Gunther Stein's report to the Christian Science Monitor regarding Japanese internal conditions and censorship deletions up to September 1943.
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Gauss forwards a copy of an exclusive press report by Gunther Stein based on information from a Chinese graduate of Fukuoka Imperial University employed by General Wang Peng-sheng. The enclosed text describes the growth of defeatism among educated Japanese after the loss of Attu and German reverses, coupled with widespread civilian dread of air raids on flammable cities. It details ambitious Japanese plans to boost monthly aircraft production to 2,500 by summer 1944, extensive factory conversions, severe rationing of rice and daily necessities, and strict military drilling of students and professionals. Passages deleted by Chinese censors, which touched on fascist leader Seigo Nakano's death, the Emperor, and Japanese fear of Russia, are also noted.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2076: Exclusive Press Report by Mr. Guenther Stein to Christian Science Monitor on Conditions in Japan Prior to September 1943

subfiles.about: Internal State Department memorandum recommending that Far Eastern Affairs officers read the valuable intelligence on Japanese conditions contained in Drumright's Sian report.
subfiles.from: H. Merrell Benninghoff, Division of Far Eastern Affairs (Japanese Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Benninghoff recommends FE read Drumright's Sian interview with student Chiao Wen-sheng as among the most useful 1943 accounts of Japanese civilian morale.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Conditions in Japan During 1943
subfiles.to: Officers of the Division of Far Eastern Affairs

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting Second Secretary Drumright's memorandum of conversation with Chinese student Chiao Wen-sheng concerning domestic conditions, student inductions, and Allied POW dock labor in Japan.
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Gauss transmits Sian Despatch No. 11 from Everett F. Drumright, enclosing a detailed memorandum of an interview with Chiao Wen-sheng, who studied in Tokyo until October 26, 1943. Chiao reports that educated Japanese recognize ultimate defeat is inevitable while rural populations remain misled by military propaganda, though grim determination to die for the Emperor persists. The report documents the military conscription of non-science students over 21, the removal of coastal populations, severe shortages of food, leather, and consumer goods, and widespread replacement of male workers by women. Crucially, Chiao reports observing over 200 thin Caucasian war prisoners performing forced coolie labor unloading iron ore flatcars under armed guard on the docks at Niigata.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2109: Conditions in Japan prior to November 1943

subfiles.about: Duplicate carbon copy of Despatch No. 2109 and its accompanying Sian memorandum detailing Japanese internal conditions prior to November 1943.
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.summary: This subfile contains a duplicate copy of Ambassador Gauss's Despatch No. 2109 and Everett F. Drumright's Sian Despatch No. 11 with its enclosed memorandum of conversation with Chiao Wen-sheng. It reproduces verbatim the comprehensive survey of conditions in Japan, emphasizing the growing fear of Russian and American industrial power, the rigid suppression of free speech by plainclothes police, and severe civilian rationing. The text describes the departure of thousands of impoverished Japanese emigrants to Manchuria from Niigata and the tight security checks at Rashin and Shanhaikuan to catch draft evaders. Chiao concludes that worsening economic privation and internal friction between military and political factions could bring down the Tojo cabinet within a year.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2109: Conditions in Japan prior to November 1943 (Duplicate Copy)

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram reporting Soviet press summaries of Japanese tax increases and major personnel changes in the Imperial Army and Navy General Staffs.
subfiles.from: W. Averell Harriman, American Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.summary: Harriman relays Moscow press on 29 new Japanese tax laws and command changes: Tojo as Army Chief of Staff, Shimada replacing Nagano in the Navy, and Iida's central-district command.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 588 from Moscow on Japanese Legislative Measures and Military High Command Changes

subfiles.about: Memorandum transmitting the minutes and approved text of the interagency Ad Hoc Committee's political directive for U.S. military government in the Japanese Mandated Islands.
subfiles.from: Abbot Low Moffat, Liberated Areas Division, Department of State
subfiles.summary: Abbot Low Moffat circulates the minutes of the January 20, 1944 meeting of the interagency Ad Hoc Committee of the Naval Office for Occupied Areas, attended by State, War, and Navy representatives at the Pentagon. The committee reviewed and amended a 14-article political directive for military government in the Japanese Mandated Islands of the Central Pacific, expanding its scope beyond the Caroline Islands to supersede the earlier Marshall Islands directive. Key provisions include suspending Japanese courts while preserving native chiefs' summary judicial powers over minor offenses, interned or segregated Japanese nationals receiving Geneva Convention protections, and treating Koreans and Chinese distinctly as liberated peoples. The directive also mandates removing Japanese language instruction from native schools and strictly prohibits flogging or cruel punishments.
subfiles.title: Memorandum and Minutes of the Meeting of the Ad Hoc Committee to Consider the Proposed Political Directive for the Military Government of the Japanese Mandated Islands in the Central Pacific
subfiles.to: John K. Johansen, Division of Far Eastern Affairs, Department of State

subfiles.about: Diplomatic telegram summarizing Soviet press reports on difficulties in Japanese urban population evacuation, new indirect taxes, and increasing Soviet coverage of the Pacific war.
subfiles.from: W. Averell Harriman, American Embassy, Moscow
subfiles.summary: Harriman reports Japanese press frustration over slow industrial decentralization and evacuation amid Marshall Islands threats, new consumer/entertainment taxes, and growing Soviet press coverage of Japan's internal strain.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 649 from Moscow on Japanese Urban Evacuation Difficulties and Tax Increases

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting Sian Despatch No. 26 and Drumright's intelligence memorandum compiling data on Japanese public morale, air defenses, airfields, and Korean agricultural labor.
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Gauss transmits Despatch No. 26 from Second Secretary Everett F. Drumright at Sian, enclosing an intelligence memorandum based on indirect reports from a Chinese student who left Japan in September 1943. The memorandum outlines the emergence of public anxiety following the defeat at Attu, withdrawal from Kiska, and the death of Admiral Yamamoto, noting pervasive fear of incendiary air raids and the widespread use of political thought police. It provides detailed intelligence on civilian air raid precautions, aviation cadet training under General Doihara, and the locations of military airfields including Tokorozawa, Haneda, Tsuchiura, and Gannosu. It further records the presence of 1,500,000 Korean agricultural laborers brought to Japan, point values for clothing rationing, and an Allied POW camp at Zentsuji where prisoners perform farm labor under academic supervision.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2167: Conditions in Japan Prior to September, 1943

subfiles.about: Duplicate hectograph copy of Despatch No. 2167 and accompanying Sian memorandum regarding Japanese internal conditions, air raid defense, and military aviation.
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.summary: This subfile is a duplicate hectograph copy of Ambassador Gauss's Despatch No. 2167 and Everett F. Drumright's Sian Despatch No. 26, enclosing the memorandum of February 7, 1944. It reproduces verbatim intelligence on Japanese domestic hardships, thought control, and community firefighting organizations such as the Young Women's Corps. The document outlines military aircraft flight units, shipyard construction prioritizing wooden vessels and submarines, and government delays of six months to four years in publishing military casualty lists. It also reiterates points schedules for clothing rationing and details regarding Korean laborers forced to take Japanese names.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2167: Conditions in Japan Prior to September, 1943 (Duplicate Copy)

subfiles.about: Despatch transmitting two bulletins from the China Information Committee in Chungking detailing daily life, severe commodity shortages, and thought control in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Clarence E. Gauss, American Embassy, Chungking
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Gauss forwards two Daily Bulletins (Nos. 882 and 893) published in February 1944 by the China Information Committee of the Ministry of Information in Chungking. The first bulletin features an interview with Ying Tso, a recent Chinese graduate of Tokyo Imperial University, who describes extreme food rationing, the industrial diversion of bean curd, the confiscation of private metals and temple bells, and widespread arrests for 'dangerous thoughts' following Admiral Yamamoto's death. The second bulletin depicts daily street scenes in Tokyo, noting that women outnumber men by two-to-one, pedestrians go barefoot in rainy weather to preserve shoes from cinder-filled roads, and diners must patronize several restaurants in succession to obtain enough rice. It also highlights the drafting of men over 58 into the Citizens Militia Corps and severe travel restrictions on crowded railways.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 2271: Conditions in Japan Prior to October 1943
